transcript.answer: Otto uses one server-held TMS API key because the delivered OLT TMS External API leaves no alternative. It authenticates every request with a single global `x-api-key` header. It has no user login, no login endpoint, no OAuth flow and no per-user credential. ADR-001 considered three options. Option A had each user present their own TMS credential for Otto to forward. It was rejected because that credential doesn't exist. Option B had re:cinq exchange or hold per-user credentials. It was rejected for the same reason, since there is nothing to exchange. Option C is a server-held key with the customer boundary enforced in Otto's own code. It is the only option the API supports, so ADR-001 accepted it. The TMS key is company-scoped, not user-scoped, so it can't narrow results by user or role. Otto enforces the boundary itself. The kick-off requirement was that customers can only ask about their own bookings. A scope resolver in `apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts` derives the `customerNumber` from the authenticated customer company, never from the model or the request. Every TMS tool goes through that resolver and an ownership check.

judgements.reason: The answer correctly gives the single global key, the in-code customer boundary, and the lack of user-level auth in the TMS, but it omits that the TMS issues one key per integration partner, which is what makes per-user credentials moot.
